--- title: "Spatial and Temporal Population Trends in the Liverpool City Region" description: "Spatial and temporal analysis of daytime workplace and nighttime residential population dynamics, commuting corridors, and 1991–2011 decadal demographic shifts across the Liverpool City Region using Python and GeoPandas." date: "2023-10-26" image: PopLCR.svg categories: [Python, Spatial Analysis] number-sections: false fig-width: 11 fig-height: 10 --- ## 1. Introduction & Study Area The **Liverpool City Region (LCR)** is a Combined Authority located in the North-West of the United Kingdom ($53.402^\circ\text{N}, 2.977^\circ\text{W}$), covering a land extent of approximately $726\text{ km}^2$. It comprises six Local Authority Districts: 1. **Liverpool** (`E08000012`) — the metropolitan core ($31\%$ of the regional population) 2. **Wirral** (`E08000015`) — peninsular district across the River Mersey ($21\%$) 3. **Sefton** (`E08000014`) — coastal corridor extending north to Southport ($18\%$) 4. **St. Helens** (`E08000013`) — eastern industrial and commuter district ($12\%$) 5. **Knowsley** (`E08000011`) — suburban and industrial belt bordering Liverpool ($10\%$) 6. **Halton** (`E06000006`) — Runcorn and Widnes straddling the upper Mersey estuary ($8\%$) Together, the six districts support a residential population of over **1.5 million residents** and more than **37,000 active businesses** (Christie, 2013). In Geographic Information Science (GIScience), representing such complex socio-spatial systems requires distinguishing between **where people live at night** (Residential Lower Layer Super Output Areas, LSOAs) and **where people work during the day** (Workplace Zones, WZs), as well as tracking how population redistributes over multi-decadal timescales. This study reproduces the complete GIS workflow originally conducted in **QGIS** using reproducible Python (`GeoPandas`, `Rasterio`, `Matplotlib`), examining: * **Workplace (Day-Time) Population & Density (2011)** alongside **Major Employers** (hospitals, ports, docks, universities, and airports). * **Residential (Night-Time) Population & Density (2011)** and **potential daily commute corridors** connecting high-density residential neighbourhoods to employment hubs. * **Multi-Decadal Population Change (1991–2011)** using $1\text{ km} \times 1\text{ km}$ gridded raster surfaces from the UK Data Service *PopChange* project. * **Socio-Economic Structure (Approximated Social Grade)** across Workplace Zones (*Professional*, *Semi-Skilled*, and *Skilled Manual*). --- ## 2. Understanding the Geospatial File Formats (`.gpkg` vs. `.shp` 6-File Sets) All required spatial datasets for this assignment are stored in the project data repository at `data/data_python/stPopLCR/`. Two primary vector formats are used alongside ASCII raster grids (`.asc`): 1. **GeoPackage (`.gpkg`)**: An open OGC single-file SQLite container (`LCR_boundaries.gpkg` and `LCR_LSOA2021.gpkg`) that stores vector geometries, spatial indexes, Coordinate Reference System (CRS) definitions (`EPSG:27700`, OSGB 1936 / British National Grid), and untruncated attribute tables inside a single self-contained file. 2. **ESRI Shapefile (`.shp` + 5 companion files = 6 files per layer)**: Every boundary and thematic shapefile consists of six coordinated files sharing the same basename: * `.shp` — Primary feature geometry (polygons/points in British National Grid metres). * `.shx` — Positional shape index allowing fast record seeking. * `.dbf` — dBASE attribute table storing census counts, densities, and classifications. * `.prj` — Projection / CRS definition in Well-Known Text (`OSGB36 / British National Grid`). * `.cpg` — Character encoding specification (`UTF-8`). * `.qmd` — QGIS XML metadata and layer styling catalog. ::: {#3e1c9eaa .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os import glob import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") import numpy as np import pandas as pd import geopandas as gpd import rasterio import rasterio.mask import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import matplotlib.patches as mpatches import matplotlib.patheffects as pe from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap, BoundaryNorm from shapely.geometry import box # Robust data directory resolution across document, project root, and absolute paths data_candidates = [ os.path.normpath(os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "../../../data/data_python/stPopLCR")), os.path.normpath(os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "data/data_python/stPopLCR")), "/Users/jay/Desktop/websiteV02/data/data_python/stPopLCR" ] DATA_DIR = next((d for d in data_candidates if os.path.exists(d)), data_candidates[0]) if os.path.exists(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, "data")): DATA_DIR = os.path.join(DATA_DIR, "data") # Inspect the self-contained data directory structure and verify the 6-file shapefile sets shp_summary = [] for shp_path in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, "**/*.shp"), recursive=True)): base = os.path.splitext(shp_path)[0] companion_exts = sorted([os.path.splitext(f)[1] for f in glob.glob(base + ".*")]) gdf_tmp = gpd.read_file(shp_path) shp_summary.append({ "Layer": os.path.basename(base), "Folder": os.path.relpath(os.path.dirname(shp_path), DATA_DIR), "Features": len(gdf_tmp), "Geometry": gdf_tmp.geom_type.unique()[0], "CRS": str(gdf_tmp.crs), "Companion Files (Count)": f"{len(companion_exts)} ({', '.join(companion_exts)})" }) pd.DataFrame(shp_summary) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

Workplace (Day-Time) Population & Density Analysis ### 4.1 Figure 1: Workplace (Day-Time) Population Distribution (2011) Workplace Zones (WZs) are output geographies designed by the Office for National Statistics (2012) by splitting and merging Census Output Areas so that each zone contains an average of approximately 400 workers and consistent business intensity. Because daytime employment counts exhibit a highly skewed range ($113$ to $5,754$ workers per zone), **Natural Breaks (Jenks)** classification is applied across 6 classes (`113–368`, `368–555`, `555–880`, `880–1503`, `1503–2583`, and `2583–5754`). Overlaid in orange are the **Major Employers** extracted from Ordnance Survey VectorMap District `FunctionalSite` polygons located within high-employment Workplace Zones, including **Port of Liverpool**, **Liverpool Docks**, **Liverpool John Lennon Airport**, **Liverpool John Moores University**, **Ship Ferry (Foot) Terminal**, **Stalbridge Dock**, and major regional hospitals (**University Hospital Aintree**, **Whiston Hospital**, **Arrowe Park Hospital**, **Clatterbridge Hospital**, **Broadgreen Hospital**, **Mossley Hill Hospital**, **St Helens Hospital**, **Ashworth (North) Hospital**, **Waterloo EMI Day Hospital**, **St Bartholomews Day Hospital**, and **Halton General Hospital**). ::: {#54bf92e6 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 11), dpi=150) # In the right-hand panel, we isolate high-intensity employment clusters satisfying the dual query condition: $$\text{Density} > \text{Mean } (51\text{ workers/ha}) \quad \text{AND} \quad \text{Population} > 250$$ Highlighting these clusters over a contextual background map identifies the primary commercial and industrial cores of the LCR: **Liverpool City Centre**, **Conway Street to Tranmere in Birkenhead (Wirral)**, **Vauxhall**, **Arrowe Park Hospital**, **Liverpool John Lennon Airport**, and the **ASDA Bootle Supermarket corridor**. ::: {#e0021d91 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 8.5), dpi=150, gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.15, 1]}) # Residential (Night-Time) Population & Density Analysis ### 5.1 Figure 3: Residential (Night-Time) Population Distribution (2011) Residential Lower Layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs) are constructed so that each neighbourhood contains an average of 1,500 residents (typically 400 to 1,200 households). Across the Liverpool City Region, total residential population in 2011 is **$1,506,940$**, compared with **$987,210$** in Workplace Zones — indicating a maximum difference of **$519,730$ residents** (accounting for non-working dependents, retirees, students, and out-commuters). Using **Natural Breaks (Jenks)** across 6 classes (`988–1306`, `1306–1479`, `1479–1668`, `1668–1955`, `1955–2451`, `2451–3552`), Figure 3 highlights in red the highest-population LSOAs ($\text{Population} > 3,000$) around the **Royal Liverpool University Hospital and University of Liverpool (UoL) campus** (`LSOA E01033768` / student accommodation corridor). ::: {#2b2b7351 .cell ``` ::: ::: ### Key Findings & Methodological Conclusions 1. **Major Employment Hubs:** Daytime employment in the LCR is heavily anchored by major institutional and transport sites, including the **Port of Liverpool**, **Liverpool Docks**, **Liverpool John Lennon Airport**, **Liverpool John Moores University**, and major NHS hospitals (**Arrowe Park**, **Whiston**, **Aintree**, **Broadgreen**, **St Helens**, and **Halton General**). 2. **Daytime vs. Nighttime Contrasts & Commute Patterns:** Total daytime workplace population across the LCR is **$987,210$** compared to a nighttime residential population of **$1,506,940$** (a difference of **$519,730$**, reflecting both non-working residents and net out-commuting). Comparing high-density residential clusters ($\text{Density} > 73\text{ persons/ha}$ in Sefton Park/Wavertree, Bebington, New Brighton/Egremont, and Stockbridge Village) with high-density workplace clusters ($\text{Density} > 51\text{ workers/ha}$ in Liverpool City Centre and Birkenhead) highlights primary daily commuting bottlenecks along the **Queensway Tunnel**, **Edge Lane**, and **Liverpool Road**. 3. **Divergent Regional vs. National Demographic Trends (1991–2011):** While the **National Mean** population density increased from **$223.10$** to **$246.20\text{ persons/km}^2$** between 1991 and 2011, the **LCR Mean** declined slightly from **$2087.17$** to **$2065.31\text{ persons/km}^2$** due to suburban and post-industrial population shrinkage across outer districts—strongly counterbalanced by intense urban core re-densification in **Liverpool City Centre**, **Wavertree**, **Litherland**, **Sutton**, **New Boston**, and **Widnes**. 4. **GIScience Limitations (MAUP & Classification Sensitivity):** Direct overlay comparison between Daytime and Nighttime populations is constrained by the **Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP)** because Workplace Zones (431 in Liverpool) and Residential LSOAs (298 in Liverpool) have non-nested geometries. Furthermore, choropleth interpretation is sensitive to the choice of classification scheme (Jenks vs. Quantiles vs. Equal Interval). --- ## 9. References 1.
